When a piece of music — or a section within it — is described as andante, it means the music should be played at a calm, flowing, walking-pace speed. Not rushed. Not dragging. Just a steady, unhurried movement forward. Imagine the pace of someone on a relaxed but purposeful walk: moving forward naturally and comfortably, without hurrying or loitering. That is the spirit of andante music.
Where it sits among other tempos

In music, the speed of a piece is called its tempo. Composers mark their music with Italian tempo words to tell performers how fast or slow to play. These words form a rough scale from very slow to very fast, and andante sits in the moderately slow zone:

  • Very slow and heavy → Largo
  • Slow and stately → Adagio
  • Walking pace, calm and flowing → Andante ← this one
  • Moderate and steady → Moderato
  • Fast and lively → Allegro
  • Very fast → Presto

So andante is slower than moderate but noticeably faster than deeply slow. It occupies a middle-slow space that feels natural and unhurried rather than heavy or sluggish.
What andante music actually sounds and feels like

Because andante moves at a natural walking pace, each note has enough room to breathe, which makes it a tempo that carries emotional weight beautifully. Andante music tends to feel lyrical, expressive, and clear — the melody speaks with intention without rushing past you. Composers often choose andante for movements that are tender, reflective, warm, or quietly powerful. It gives the listener time to feel what the music is saying.

As an adjective, andante modifies a noun — typically a musical movement, passage, or section. Examples of how it's used:

  • "The second movement is an andante movement" — that movement should be played at a walking, unhurried pace.
  • "The andante passage of the concerto" — that passage is marked to be played at this tempo.
  • "This is an andante piece" — the entire piece flows at a walking pace.

When you see andante written at the top of a sheet of music or at the start of a section, it is a direct instruction to the performer: play this at a calm, walking-pace tempo.

Note: andante also works as a noun in practice — "the andante of the symphony" refers to the movement or section that carries this tempo marking. This is simply the word being used to name the section itself, based on its adjective label.

Composers sometimes add other words alongside andante to fine-tune the character or pace:

  • Andante cantabile — andante, but with a singing, songlike quality (cantabile means "singable"). Smooth and flowing like a vocal melody.
  • Andante con moto — andante, but with a little extra energy and movement (con moto means "with motion"). Slightly livelier than plain andante.
  • Andante maestoso — andante, but with a majestic, grand character. Stately and dignified.
  • Andante sostenuto — andante, but with notes fully held and sustained, giving a weighty, deeply expressive feel.
  • Andantino — a close relative of andante, technically its diminutive form. Historically its meaning has been debated, but in modern practice, andantino is generally understood as slightly faster than andante — a touch lighter and more delicate in movement.

Some of the most beloved passages in all of classical music are andante:

  • Mozart's Piano Concerto No. 21, second movement — marked Andante. A hauntingly beautiful, floating melody that became widely known from the 1967 Swedish film Elvira Madigan. It's a perfect example of andante at its most lyrical and expressive.
  • Beethoven's Symphony No. 5, second movement — marked Andante con moto. Warm, flowing, and gently energetic.
  • Brahms' Symphony No. 1, second movement — marked Andante sostenuto. Rich, sustained, and deeply emotional.

These examples show why composers reach for andante when they want music that communicates something meaningful and felt — the pace is unhurried enough that emotion registers fully, without the heaviness of a truly slow tempo.
Can andante describe things outside music?

Strictly speaking, andante is a musical term. However, in literary or informal writing, it occasionally appears as a figurative adjective to describe anything with a calm, measured, walking-pace quality — a film's pacing, a conversation's rhythm, or the unhurried movement of a scene. This is non-standard usage, but you may encounter it in creative writing.
The one thing to hold onto

Andante = moderately slow, at a natural walking pace, calm and flowing. It describes music that moves steadily without hurry, sits between slow (adagio) and moderate (moderato) on the tempo scale, and is associated with expressiveness, lyricism, and emotional depth.
